text: I'm also excited about more widespread engagement with the alignment problem. Whether you agree or disagree with my claims in this thread, the stakes of the situation justify robust debate and in-depth analysis. Feedback and discussion very welcome; let's figure this problem out!

author: RichardMCNgo
text: How can we prevent AGI misalignment? I'm most excited about work on scalable oversight (theory: https://t.co/LZqCPtcD0D; practice: https://t.co/i3HreKCpyf) and mechanistic interpretability (https://t.co/Jq68YXXAas). See this curriculum for more: https://t.co/FZklkurzz7

author: RichardMCNgo
text: It's hard to predict what happens next. But once AGIs are working against us, I'm not optimistic. The historical record shows that whoever produces the best tech (by this point, AGIs themselves) comes to dominate the world. One way that might happen: https://t.co/D84xf9xJ47

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Fundamentally these are claims about inductive biases, which wouldn't apply to a lookup-table "AGI". But realistic AGIs will do instrumental reasoning, which will bias them towards power-seeking generalization - like preventing us from shutting them down. https://t.co/moFhCP0Rcq

author: RichardMCNgo
text: This is a form of goal misgeneralization: https://t.co/W0RX49xnUt. AGIs will understand that that “obey humans in a non-manipulative way” is one possible generalization of “obey humans”—but almost no other possible generalizations will rule out power-seeking manipulation.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: We'll try to train AGIs to follow constraints like honesty, but that won't scale as they become superhuman. Analogously, an adult constrained to be honest can still persuade a child to approve of actions which are very harmful, like eating food which happens to be poisonous.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Turner et al. formalize the intuitive claim that power-seeking is often very useful. So while we can’t predict which misaligned goals AGIs will develop, AGIs will likely find power-seeking strategies which achieve those goals by disempowering humans. https://t.co/R0rWrPM1C5

author: RichardMCNgo
text: But by Bostrom's instrumental convergence thesis (https://t.co/mxE81Eww7y), almost all large-scale goals lead to instrumental goals like survival, resource acquisition, etc - just because these are so robustly useful. As Russell puts it, you can’t fetch coffee if you’re dead!

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Situationally-aware policies will be able to get higher reward by deliberately exploiting our mistakes - e.g. by lying about their goals, trying to earn our trust, etc. Advanced AIs will be very good at modelling humans (there's a lot of data!) so this will be hard to catch.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: 2. Some goals are instrumentally useful across many environments (curiosity, making money, etc) which will teach policies to value them. If they're correlated with reward often enough, policies may rarely see data which teaches them to prioritize alignment over these other goals.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: The policy was trained with human feedback to grab a ball, but learned to hold the claw between camera and ball to fool evaluators. This example is trivial, but consistent errors might teach policies to try to *seem* helpful rather than *being* helpful. https://t.co/VAsEQ7F72t

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
But these examples are all task-specific; why might misaligned goals correlate with reward across many tasks, and generalize to new tasks? Consider two broad reasons:
1. Consistent flaws in our evaluation procedures. E.g. can you spot the problem in this gif? https://t.co/cE4qkjsPVj

author: RichardMCNgo
text: The goals policies learn will depend on the reward functions we train them on. Krakovna et al. give many examples of misspecified rewards which lead to a range of misbehavior - RL learns to exploit even very subtle misspecifications! https://t.co/joS2JksW8j

author: RichardMCNgo
text: I'm unsure if existing networks have goals in this sense. But Jaderberg et al find neurons that "code directly for important game states" in their deep RL policy. It seems very likely that AGIs will use high-level outcome-representations to choose actions. https://t.co/GTfOUDyFEh

In the report I outline an illustrative deep reinforcement learning training setup, then discuss three phases of training I expect to see:

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Alignment arguments are often very abstract because we lack empirical data or solid theory for AGI. But that's exactly why the problem seems hard to solve, and why we should work to build those theories in advance! If we don't, we may have little time to catch up as we near AGI.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: To start, why think about this now? ML progress has been astonishingly rapid over the last decade. And surveys show many top ML researchers expect AGI within decades. So if misalignment is plausible we should do our best to understand the core problem. https://t.co/EhJrNKEvpc

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
Advantages of one-off selection:
- once in, people can feel secure and abundant, which helps them do great things
- the best people are self-motivated

Disadvantages:
- the stronger the selection, the more performance on the proxy diverges from what you care about
- people change

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
A question on my mind: when you're optimizing for a metric using imperfect proxies, when is it better to do one-off strong selection, vs continual weak selection?

The former is like Harvard or Google (getting in is the hardest part). Most other jobs are the latter.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
Intuitively, if cooperation leads to the best outcomes, won't highly capable superorganisms figure that out?

But we have no idea what the offense-defense balance converges to, or what internal constraints they'll face at those scales. They may also vary much more than humans do.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
One way the future will be more coordinated: we'll build very large "superorganisms", like multistellar civilisations.

But the largest future superorganisms might still not cooperate with each other very much, just as modern superpowers often work against each other.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
To summarize my values, I care about:
- the welfare of all beings, present and future (intrinsic care-morality)
- the agency of all currently-existing beings (intrinsic cooperation-morality)
- being cooperative in order to achieve these (instrumental cooperation-morality) 7/8

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Since it’s so hard to deduce the instrumental benefits of cooperation-morality, evolution made us care intrinsically about cooperative principles, which carries over even to cases where they're no longer useful. So cooperation is more than just an instrumental strategy. 6/8

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
Because
A) Like in economics, the benefits come via complex multi-agent dynamics
B) We reason using causal decision theories which don't account for others predicting our actions. Cooperation is more intuitively useful under functional decision theory: https://t.co/303VTASxPc 5/8

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
Many intuitions which seem strange from a care-morality view make more sense under cooperation-morality, like:
- The act-omission distinction
- Person-affecting population ethics
- Deontological rules 

Why is it hard to deduce the instrumental benefits of these intuitions? 4/8

author: RichardMCNgo
text: When you’re in a multi-agent environment, though, others respond to your choices in complex ways which make cooperation-morality instrumentally useful. E.g. a rule of absolute honesty is instrumentally useful if others can predict when you’ll lie. https://t.co/Zk6DS5s0Rr 3/8

author: RichardMCNgo
text: An extreme example of care-morality is hedonic utilitarianism, which only treats others as moral patients, not moral agents. Care-morality implicitly assumes your decisions are the only thing that matter. In one sense that’s true: your actions are all you can affect. 2/8

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Many conflicts between ethical intuitions arise from failing to distinguish between morality as care vs morality as cooperation. Care-morality means looking after others’ welfare. Cooperation-morality means upholding their agency, e.g. by not deceiving or disempowering them. 1/8

My current guess is that conscious valence (e.g. pleasure, pain) arises because brain modularity necessitates internal conflict.

If our neocortices were cleverer and more aligned with the rest of our brain, they wouldn't need to be blasted with valence to steer them.

author: RichardMCNgo

Just realized that as the world gets bigger and more chaotic, this effect becomes increasingly important.

As people feel less and less powerful, they assume someone else must benefit. But it's not zero-sum: coordination difficulties can reduce everyone's control over the world.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
I used to phrase this as: "you can only have what you want if you're not trying too hard to get it".

To goal-oriented people, this can feel like an unsolvable koan. My past self hated it. But as my new phrasing suggests, it can be solved via introspection, self-love and honesty.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
The secret to so many human interactions is: it doesn't matter what you do as long as those actions aren't coming from hidden neediness.

I say "hidden" because openly and honestly acknowledging neediness is surprisingly powerful at reducing it. Sunlight is the best disinfectant.

quoted.text: A really undervalued trait: epistemic paranoia. Sure, you may know that your brain is biased. But do you really viscerally believe that it's *out to get you* - that even your most fundamental frameworks may be totally wrong?

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @RomeoStevens76 @xuenay Agree I'm writing the bottom line, but I don't know what the alternative is. Anyone I see who is not paranoid about seeking truth ends up going off the rails when exploring intellectual frontiers. I can afford to trade off other things but not that, given my skills and goals.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
@RomeoStevens76 @xuenay The intellectual part which has objections is exactly the part which is being asked to step back. Without that idk if pushback happens.

I don't expect wild divergence but I do expect increasing entropy as more and more random narratives get hooked into my epistemology.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @AmmannNora Then I wonder: why do I think I'm so fragile that I can't handle a few false narratives hooking into my emotions? I don't feel fragile usually. A part of me thinks that bad stuff gets unleashed when I give up control. Another part can't separate "listening" and "believing".

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @AmmannNora I think my concern is less any specific deception and more a general trend towards entropy. As I do more IFS I generate more and more narratives, and most are reasonable but some are wack. The intellectual part will always doubt them but maybe they'll hook into emotions anyway.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @xuenay Poking at this more, it's something like "narratives are self-fulfilling, goddammit, why would you let random brain parts generate them in a context where the only ground truth is whether or not something feels good?!"

author: RichardMCNgo

@xuenay Mm, okay. This does seems sensible, but there's a part of me that is *really* scared of getting fooled at all while doing IFS - it feels like as soon as I loosen my grip, I'll be able to convince myself of anything.

This might just be a control neurosis, idk.

Ultimately I don't think any of these tradeoffs are unavoidable; you can always find ways to get both at once.

But that requires energy/agency/talent, which is always in short supply. So maybe the most fundamental tradeoff is "empowering people" vs "just doing stuff yourself".

author: RichardMCNgo
text: The last one can plausibly be solved by applying more emotional intelligence: you can make people feel understood and cared for without agreeing that you should shift your focus (although that's more a 1:1 move - doing it publicly is hard to distinguish from conceding the point).

- cringiness fights drift to status-seeking

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Those three stand out as the most widespread and egregious incompetence on standard political issues. Other contenders include pollution, education, overregulation, and incarceration. These are less straightforward to fix than the first three, but that's not saying much!

author: RichardMCNgo
text: You can think of difficulty in terms of searching for hypotheses. Even explaining in detail why X is wrong still leaves open any possibility apart from X. Saying "Y is underrated" specifies a broad direction. Saying "here's how Y works" requires constructing a whole new theory.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
Important to remember that it's *much* easier to identify flaws in other people's ideas than to construct correct ideas yourself.

In particular, "people overrate X" is easier than "people underrate Y" is easier than "I know how Y works".

author: RichardMCNgo
text: A counterargument: males in some species don’t compete via shows of force - e.g. birds which sing to attract mates. Maybe this is because 90% of birds are monogamous, though (vs <5% of mammals), which promotes labour specialisation. Do all non-monogamous males compete physically?

author: RichardMCNgo
text: If true, it feels a bit sad: there could be a much better solution if it weren’t for the threat of physical force. But it does seem pretty plausible to me - especially because hermaphroditism is much more common in plants, which can’t use the strategy of physical dominance.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
6. Physical dominance.

Maybe male competition is grounded in physical power, so dominant males could just prevent hermaphrodites (who invest less in muscle and brawn) from impregnating anyone. So sexes aren't a solution to an environmental problem, but to a coordination problem.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: This effect plausibly occurs in plants (https://t.co/n60jrM3eiF) but not strongly enough to prevent most of them from being hermaphroditic. Maybe the plant-animal divergence is driven by a combination of this and the previous options. But I think the 6th option is the strongest:

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
5. Self-fertilisation

Perhaps self-fertilisation has a strong short-term advantage, despite losing out on the long-term benefits of sex (https://t.co/J47rIKwQg8). If hermaphrodites often evolve ways to self-fertilise, group selection could prevent hermaphroditism from spreading.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: But on timeframes where sexual desires can themselves evolve, we should expect stabilising sexual selection towards the best combination of fertility and attractiveness. I.e. why doesn't everyone end up most attracted to whoever seems like the best hermaphrodite?

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
4. Difficulty of fixating hermaphroditism.

A hermaphrodite in a species without many hermaphrodites is likely not as attractive to females as most males are, nor as fertile as most females are. So maybe even after arising in a few individuals, the trait will be selected against.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
3. Difficulty of evolving hermaphroditism.

But non-reproductive hermaphroditism arises via mutations pretty frequently, so I’d be surprised if reproductive hermaphroditism were unachievable. And there are a few hermaphroditic animals - so why haven’t they spread more widely?

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
2. Developmental or metabolic costs of being hermaphroditic.

Maybe having two sets of functional sex organs is just a very expensive adaptation? But this seems unlikely to be the main factor - the relevant baseline is the existence of males at all, which is a huge energy cost.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
1. Specialisation of labour

If there’s a strong division of labour between males and females, maybe it’s harder for hermaphrodites to gather enough resources to support offspring. But in many species males contribute little - eg orang-utans, who are very solitary.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: And in fact, most plants are hermaphroditic - so why aren’t animals, apart from a handful? A quick search doesn’t turn up any widely accepted answer, so I’ve brainstormed a few possibilities. I’m not a biologist and may well be missing something big; if so, please let me know.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: It's pretty clear why sex itself happens - gene exchange is very valuable (e.g. see https://t.co/9Owql5mUUh). But a species with only hermaphrodites could get all the genetic benefits of sex, without the massive cost of half its population being unable to bear offspring.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
One thing I really like about evolutionary biology is that many seemingly-basic questions are still areas of active research.

Here’s one I’ve been thinking about, which I haven’t seen a satisfactory answer to: evolutionarily speaking, why aren’t we all hermaphrodites?

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Perhaps it’s worth considering what differences you’d expect in a world where this is true vs false. (For example, might you expect that the highest-status men actually don’t spend much time dancing, drinking, or even socialising?) 16/N

author: RichardMCNgo
text: If I were more cynical I'd say that the “fun” part of high-status fun is also a strategic ambiguity to facilitate status transactions - if people couldn’t convince themselves and others that they were having fun, their attempts to seem prestigious would be much more obvious. 15/N

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Basically the same dynamics play out internationally as well - promoters offer girls free flights, food and accommodation in exchange for attendance at nightclubs in St Tropez, etc. On those trips the transactionality is usually a bit more obvious. 14/N

author: RichardMCNgo
text: In some sense the whole system is grounded in the models’ sex appeal, but I think the models’ prestige is just as important - models are preferred to women who most men find more attractive, as well as preferred to women who have more transactional attitudes towards sex. 13/N

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Promoters are disproportionately black; Mears talks about them having “colour capital”, and using some stereotypes to their advantage in order to catch attention. They need to be very charismatic and attractive to convince girls to come along without seeming transactional. 12/N

author: RichardMCNgo
text: The nightclub profits by creating an atmosphere of “suspended reality” where a large group of people who all individually believe that buying status in this way is tacky can still convince themselves that all the other people don’t think it’s tacky. 11/N

author: RichardMCNgo
text: The markup on champagne is determined not by the amount of champagne, but by how ostentatious the purchase is. The biggest purchases, costing >100k per bottle, come with elaborate fanfare: all music stops, spotlights shine on the buyer, a train of staff bring it out, etc. 10/N

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
Everyone selects for models even when they don’t personally find the model look attractive, because the fashion industry established it as the Schelling look for high-status women. (For more, see Mears’ other book, Pricing Beauty; and my tweet below.) 9/N
https://t.co/RvSiKRTQZq

quoted.text:

author: RichardMCNgo
text: At a top club, a promoter might get paid $1000 a night to bring out a dozen models or women who look like models. Notably, model-like beauty is much more highly-prized than conventional beauty - e.g. the clubs don’t allow access to women who aren’t unusually tall. 8/N

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
(I’m strongly reminded of Michael Sandel’s book What Money Can’t Buy - the intuitions about the corrosive effects of money are the same here, just applied to a much less high-minded setting.) https://t.co/EfgZEyKOnh

Some other interesting observations: 7/N

author: RichardMCNgo
text: And most are careful not to ruin their reputations by accepting cash from promoters. Instead, to bring enough girls, promoters each need to do a bunch of emotional labour, flirting, relationship-building, and many non-cash payments (food, transport, even accommodation). 6/N

author: RichardMCNgo
text: The nightclubs pay “promoters” to scout out and bring along dozens of beautiful women each night. Those women get access to an exclusive venue with many wealthy men - but by itself that’s not enough to motivate regular attendance, at least not from the prettiest. 5/N

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
Instead an ecosystem develops to sell sufficient strategic ambiguity to allow (self- and other-) deception about the transaction taking place, by incorporating a series of middlemen.

To start, men pay thousands for table charges and already-expensive drinks at 5-20x markups. 4/N

author: RichardMCNgo
text: But explicit transactions between different forms of cultural capital are low-status - it demonstrates that you can’t get the other forms directly. So the wealthy men can’t just pay the beautiful women to come party with them. 3/N

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Some activities which are often fun - dancing, drinking, socialising - become much more fun when you're also feeling high-status. So wealthy men want to buy the feeling of high-status fun, by partying alongside other high-status people, particularly beautiful women. 2/N

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
New York’s nightclubs are the particle accelerators of sociology: reliably creating precise conditions under which exotic extremes of status-seeking behaviour can be observed.

author: RichardMCNgo

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @BasilHalperin The same is true for "if I cooperate, he cooperates" - you just need to understand it as a higher-level intervention, over not just your decision but rather the common factor between your decision and his decision (namely, your shared decision algorithm).

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @BasilHalperin Your atom-level response is too strong because it rules out normal counterfactuals too. When I say "if I'd never joined twitter, then X" the antecedent may be physically impossible - since I did join twitter! But we can understand it as a claim about a higher-level intervention.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
@BasilHalperin The intuition here is that even *after* you are cloned, you are able to (correctly) reason "if I cooperate he will cooperate, and if I don't he won't".

This reasoning doesn't make sense under classical counterfactuals. Since it works, we need a better notion of counterfactuals.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
@BasilHalperin I don't think Yudkowsky et al are making the mistake you identify.

You can see this by removing the time component - e.g. consider playing a prisoner's dilemma with a perfect duplicate of yourself. What response do you endorse there?

author: RichardMCNgo

@NathanpmYoung I think in all of the cases I mentioned having the "right reasons" is a terminal value, whereas in your examples it's an instrumental value.

For AI, technically it's an instrumental value too, but there's something about the terminality that I want to capture in the analogy.

author: RichardMCNgo

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Here's the win-win strategy: MIT and other top unis should aim to push the frontiers of how amazing online educational content can be. They're already doing well, but each professor should have a whole team of professionals helping with course design. They have the money for it!

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Now, staying small and having low acceptance rates also keeps them prestigious and high-ranked. Net effect unclear - it's good for science and intellectuals to be more prestigious in wider society, but it also normalises the proliferation of expensive, time-consuming degrees.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: If the main value that top unis provide to society is creating hubs for extreme talent, these considerations suggest they should remain small and selective for in-person students, while spreading high-quality teaching online. Which, interestingly, is what they're doing!

author: RichardMCNgo
text: On the other hand, this means most students won't be far from the median. So the marginal additional acceptance will seem pretty similar to existing students, but plausibly drag down the mean much more than expected if you weren't accounting for long tails.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
I intermittently hear claims like "Most MIT students have topped their classes their whole lives, and suddenly half of them are below average."

I think that's an underestimate - *most* MIT students are below average. MIT admits a long tail at the top, but not at the bottom.

text:
This shouldn't be surprising, because it's how scientists often discover new phenomena. But it's easy to assume that the interface adds so much it can't be sidestepped.

Same for business - big corps are the standard interface for doing stuff, but entrepreneurs see past that.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Concrete example: science is an interface for learning about the world. It's one of the most successful interfaces ever, featuring many valuable tools, norms and methods. Yet in many domains you can still move beyond scientific knowledge by playing around with what interests you.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: There's a systematic reason for this: creating interfaces that map onto the structure of reality is really hard, and preserving them under competitive pressure even harder. So there are cracks in everything. But few people are looking for them, because that's effortful and weird.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Modern society often feels like many layers of interfaces between individuals and reality. But reality is usually much more accessible than you expect - if you bypass the interfaces you can just reach out, touch it, and make things happen.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
@iamtrask Well, during the time we were diverging from chimps we never did math; we never built skyscrapers; we never flew planes; we never led armies; we never wrote books; we never did science.

Insofar as we can do all these things now it's because we evolved skills that generalise.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @iamtrask So abstraction, like planning, is another thing which just needs to be learned once. Add a few more things in this category and suddenly your system has most of what it needs to be a general intelligence.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @iamtrask The way that humans model the whole world is by having representations at many different levels of abstraction. On some tasks you only need a few levels of abstraction ("forget about everything outside this chess game"). On most, though, understanding wider context helps a lot.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @iamtrask I really hope you're right, because that'd prevent the worst alignment problems. But if you were right, I don't think we'd have been able to build civilisation in the first place, because humans rely so much on skills generalised from our wildly different ancestral environment.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @iamtrask Uncertain about this example mainly because chess is plausibly too simple and divorced from the real world for such transfer to be useful. But very few of the tasks we're interested in are like that!

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @iamtrask Oh, interesting. I'm uncertain about this specific example but in general I expect core skills like reasoning, planning, language, etc to be useful for a very wide range of tasks. See how humans beat beavers at building dams, beat birds at navigation, beat lions at hunting, etc.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @shakked_noy Even if the core questions are phrased in nonempirical ways, I expect that the fastest and most reliable way to make progress on them is to develop a very good empirical understanding of related topics. That's worked very well so far.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Another example: I've been surprised by the extent to which top ML researchers choose research directions based on philosophical assumptions. But without channels to share those ideas widely, everyone has to develop them separately, which makes it much harder to improve them.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: The situation where I expect this problem most strongly is incubating new fields, because it often requires informal observation, tinkering, "huh that's weird", etc - all unpublishable! So the branches of science which dominate the 21st century will likely start with blog posts.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Another example: statistical tools have been very useful for many disciplines to better analyse data. But the use of p-values, etc, has become so embedded that even though we have better options, we can't switch to them, because people think of p-values as the standard of rigor.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: studying traditionally philosophical topics - minds, consciousness, ethics, etc - open up, philosophers have been slow to embrace them, because what now defines the field is not the subject matter but rather a certain (incomplete) type of rigor.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: One example: "philosophy" used to include many empirical subfields, such as the natural sciences. As other fields split off, analytic philosophers embraced a style of nonempirical rigor. This was crucial in preventing them from falling into postmodernism! But as empirical ways of

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Many academics are very careful about intellectual rigor, e.g. ignoring informal blog posts. I deeply respect that caution. But holding too tightly to any given conception of rigor closes you off from improving the way you seek truth - which severely inhibits long-term progress.

text: @pwillsit A tells B a budget. B can assign some of B's own budget to C, if they choose. A never needs to interact with C.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
@pwillsit It's A's responsibility to assign share budgets to B and C separately which add up to less than the total share budget A intends.

Under some norms, B and C could then agree to trade share budgets. (Which norm is better to use depends on how similar the people they'd tell are.)

author: RichardMCNgo
text: @keithwynroe Oh, so each box can be thought of as specifying some set of reals - namely, all the reals that appear later on in the chain. And now we have countably many sets of countably many reals. Definitely seems like something we can use choice on - but to what end?

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
@keithwynroe So now each box can be thought of as specifying a real number via links to other boxes. Does this get us anywhere?

Feels like the 100 is a red herring, if you can solve with 100 you can solve with 2. To use axiom of choice we want to set up infinitely many equivalence classes.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
@keithwynroe Okay, let me just brainstorm out loud for a bit.
First define some function from reals to boxes. E.g. "invert then round down".
Then each box points to another box.
Now define a function from chains of boxes to reals. E.g. "append 0 if box number is even, append 1 otherwise".

Not saying the latter narrative is true; even if you think AI will produce the most innovation going forward, there are such big failures in other domains that the stagnation lens is often useful.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
Diagnosing stagnation is hard because it's not just an evaluation, but also a prediction: that the sectors we've prioritised aren't effective investments in the future.

"We don't get flying cars because innovation in atoms is broken" vs "we've found more important stuff to do".

author: RichardMCNgo
text: If a social media platform gave scientists a lot of status based on posts about their scientific achievements, that'd be great. It wouldn't reward work on the platform much, but it'd reward much more valuable work off it. (Google Scholar kinda does this, and LinkedIn a bit too.)

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Now, usually regarding the creation of value is better than rewarding the showcasing of value, because it rewards productivity and helps disrupt existing hierarchies. But it depends a lot on the type of value in each case, and what effort put into pursuing that value displaces.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
TikTok and YouTube are far on the proof of work end: everyone needs to put in a huge amount of work, and so the advantage from having existing status is much lower.

That's why they've created many more internet celebrities than any of the other platforms I mentioned.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
Proof of work creates value. Proof of stake showcases value. LinkedIn is the purest proof of stake platform; nobody's there for the content.

Instagram and Twitter are in the middle - you put work into posts, but they often rely on existing traits (beauty, interestingness, etc).

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
There's a fantastic essay by @eugenewei about how social media platforms provide "status as a service" via "proof of work". If you haven't read it yet, you definitely should: https://t.co/PtI420mE3p

Riffing off that: I think we can extend the analogy to cover proof of stake too.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: My key argument here: humans were optimised very hard by evolution for achieving goals, and much less hard for intellectual research. So if we optimise AIs for the latter, then when they first surpass us at that, it seems unlikely that they'll be as agentic as we are now.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: 3. Now, as AIs get more intelligent I agree that they'll eventually become arbitrarily agentic. But the key question (which Scott unfortunately omits) is: will early superhuman intelligences be worryingly agentic? If they're not, we can use them to do superhuman safety research.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: In this frame, making a tool AI into a consequentialist agent is therefore less like "connect model to output device" and more like "give model many new skills involving motivation, attention, coherence, metacognition, etc". Which seems much less likely to happen by accident.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Thinking in terms of "motivational systems" makes agency less binary. We all know humans who are very smart and very lazy. And the space of AI minds is much broader, so we should expect that it contains very smart AIs that are much less goal-directed than low-motivation humans.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: 2. Scott describes non-agentic AI as one which "doesn’t realize the universe exists, or something to that effect? It just likes connecting premises to conclusions." A framing I prefer: an AI that's very good at pattern-matching but lacks a well-developed motivational system.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: 1. Scott describes my position as similar to Eric Drexler's CAIS framework. But Drexler's main focus is modularity, which he claims leads to composite systems that aren't dangerously agentic. Whereas I instead expect unified non-modular AGIs; for more, see https://t.co/ZqroJLpwIN

author: RichardMCNgo
text: I do think most people should aim to make their best friendships significantly more committed. Maybe this is inconsistent. But ideally what you get out of a close, committed friendship is quite different from what you get out of a 2nd relationship (e.g. no messy sexual dynamics).

author: RichardMCNgo
text: The original argument also weighs against committing hard to friends and family. But very few people commit to friends anywhere near as strongly as partners (e.g. living with them indefinitely). And strong commitments to parents do strain relationships (esp. in asian families).

author: RichardMCNgo
text: A few other points that come to mind: I think people in my circles are unusually good at the type of communication which makes relationships thrive. But they're also unusually individualistic and career-focused, so maybe this cancels out overall?

author: RichardMCNgo

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
And a counterresponse: sure, but that's high-variance! If very deep commitment is so crucial, why tempt fate through actions which invoke many of our strongest and most unreasonable instincts?

OTOH if there's any experience which makes that risk worthwhile, it's falling in love.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: To me the most compelling response is that, done well, poly strengthens commitment, by making you work through a series of tricky trust exercises. (This response is more applicable to hierarchical than non-hierarchical poly relationships, but the former seem much more common.)

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Imo the best argument against polyamory, which I've seldom heard, is not about love or sex, but rather commitment. You can't have two top priorities, and I'd guess returns to more commitment and psychological safety remain very high well past the point most relationships reach.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
I think it can be, if you're scared of people rejecting you for your openness.

But the fact that vulnerability and openness come apart at the tails (especially for people who are naturally very high openness) is an important one which took me a long time to learn!

text: @jackinlondon Oh, absolutely! So maybe better to think of this as the stages of acquiring subskills or facets of a larger skill, rather than acquiring mastery over a whole domain.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
Four stages of learning a skill:
1. unconsciously wrong
2. consciously wrong
3. consciously right
4. unconsciously right

Going from 1 to 2 feels like noticing confusion; from 2 to 3, like walking a tightrope; from 3 to 4, like entering a flow state.

text: If the first months of each job were explicitly called "training time" then many fewer people would feel like imposters. But since the fastest training is real-world experience, it often looks like flailing and failing. Just remember: the optimal amount of that is more than zero!

The best person for the job is often one who will grow into the role.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: To be clear, though, I think the boundary between self-deception and self-aware lying is very fuzzy. Much self-deception seems more like motivated-looking-away-even-though-you-kinda-already-know-what's-there than a properly subconscious/unconscious phenomenon.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: This parallels a more common defence of deontology: that it prevents bad actors from justifying misbehavior to others via deception. But in most social circles self-deception is much more prevalent than self-aware lying, so I think the frame from my previous tweet is underrated.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: A frame I've been playing with: old-fashioned deontological morality was adaptive in large part because it prevented people from justifying misbehavior via self-deception. Attempts to reason our way to new social norms will be flawed unless we explicitly engage with this problem.
